request.system: You are an expert in clinical classification systems.

messages.content:
ICD-10-AM is the Australian modification of the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th revision. Its disease codes are arranged in chapters, and a three-character category is written as one capital letter followed by two digits. The letter indicates the chapter or block: A and B are infectious diseases, C is malignant neoplasms, D is other neoplasms and blood disorders, E is endocrine, nutritional and metabolic disease, F is mental and behavioural disorders, G is the nervous system, H is the eye and ear, I is the circulatory system, J is the respiratory system, K is the digestive system, L is the skin, M is the musculoskeletal system, N is the genitourinary system, O is pregnancy and childbirth, P is the perinatal period, Q is congenital malformations, R is symptoms and abnormal findings, S and T are injury and poisoning, and Z is factors influencing health status. The two digits narrow the chapter to a specific category, for example J44 is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and N17 is acute kidney failure.

The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Using that structure, assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. Choose the chapter letter first, then the two digits.

Hospital course:
Hospital Course:

The patient is a 67-year-old male who presented with an enlarging heterogeneous mass in the right upper lobe and shortness of breath with activity. On examination, he had a grade 3-4 of 6 holosystolic murmur. Imaging studies including Echography, Computed tomography (CT), bone scintigraphy, and Positron Emission Tomography (PET) identified the pulmonary malignancy, classified as T2N0M0. An electrocardiogram (ECG) showed severe prolapse of the posterior mitral leaflet with flail of the middle scallop (P2, P3 segment), with severe mitral regurgitation and New York Heart Association (NYHA) class II. The patient elected to have a one-stage ipsilateral Video-Assisted Thoracic Surgery (VATS) and minimally invasive cardiac surgery.
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Treatment:

The patient underwent right upper lobectomy and minimally invasive surgery (MIS) of mitral valve for definitive diagnostic and therapeutic procedures. The procedures were performed smoothly without complications. Gore-Tex loops were used for ring sizing and valve competency testing. The patient recovered well after the operation and was discharged from the hospital 10 days after the surgery.

Follow-up:

The patient did not experience any complications during follow-up.

Answer in the form CODE: <letter><digit><digit>

text:
Two conditions were treated in this episode: a lung malignancy (right upper lobe, T2N0M0) and severe mitral regurgitation from posterior leaflet prolapse and flail. Both were addressed in the same admission, so the choice depends on which was chiefly responsible.

The admission was planned as a one-stage combined procedure. The lung cancer was the enlarging mass that triggered the workup, and the lobectomy was the diagnostic and definitive treatment. The mitral valve was repaired at the same operation. Both conditions therefore had equal resource use, and neither is clearly the main reason for admission.

When two or more conditions equally meet the definition of principal diagnosis, the ICD-10-AM coding standards allow either to be sequenced first. Malignancy is usually chosen in this situation because the presentation, the imaging, and the first-listed treatment (lobectomy) all centre on the lung. The mass is also the reason the patient was investigated, and the cardiac lesion was found during that workup.

Lung cancer in the right upper lobe is coded to C34, malignant neoplasm of bronchus and lung.

CODE: C34
